title: The four other inhabited territories: their governments, electorates and statehood
usableAnswer: Per territory: offices with qualifications, terms and calendar; voter qualifications; the delegate; status-vote history with dates and results; and anything unknown marked UNKNOWN.
whyItMatters: The game seats 52 jurisdictions today (lifePlaceStateIdentities), so these four have no government, electorate or place. The owner direction says each is its own government and electorate and must never inherit a state fallback as its law, and that statehood is an ordinary political issue pursued through territorial and congressional institutions.

answer.summary: Two new files. Owner intent (revised): territory residents hold individual, changeable opinions about their own status, including uncertainty, and never inferred from geography; lamontae wants key statehood transition decisions playable, with routine steps automatic, and each admission measure controls its own legal transition. Precedent: Article IV section 3 lets Congress admit states with no universal referendum, order, waiting period or proclamation; each admission law sets its own conditions and dates. Alaska (Pub. L. 85-508, 1958) accepted a constitution voters had adopted, required elections for two senators and one representative, and took effect by presidential proclamation in January 1959, with territorial officials serving until then. Hawaii (Pub. L. 86-3, 1959) was similar, with the House temporarily at 437 until reapportionment. Neither is a template. Proposed route (a recommendation, not approved): ordinary public argument; local consent where local law provides; Congress enacts a specific measure (delegates advocate but cannot cast the final floor vote); only the elections the measure requires, with continuity until its effective date; then state authority, two senators, House seats and electors going forward. D.C. is a federal district under the 23rd Amendment and is handled separately. Earlier answer (2026-09-22T22:29:00.000Z), kept: Owner intent (from the engineering handoff): 56 inhabited jurisdictions; D.C. is a federal district, not a territory; the uninhabited Minor Outlying Islands are excluded; American Samoan nationality must not collapse into citizenship; delegates and the Resident Commissioner are not voting House members; players run through the ordinary candidacy, campaign, election, seating and governing path; statehood is an issue actors can advocate or oppose, with no scripted leader office or button, and 'fame by itself is not a vote'; residents hold varied status opinions, never inferred from geography; a statehood change applies prospectively, preserving history and seat ids; voter registration happens automatically in the background at 18 once a person otherwise qualifies (a game simplification). Research: American Samoa has a 1967 constitution (first constitutional elections 1977) and a bicameral Fono whose Senate is tied to matai custom; voters are citizens or nationals, 18 or older, with two years in the territory and one in the district; the delegate must 'owe allegiance' and be 25. Guam has a unicameral legislature and village mayors; voters are citizens at 18 with preregistration from 16; its January 1982 status plebiscite gave commonwealth 49%, statehood 26%, status quo 10%, incorporated 5%, free association 4%, independence 4%, other 2%, and the September 1982 runoff commonwealth 73% to statehood 27%; an ancestry-restricted plebiscite was struck down (Davis v. Guam, Ninth Circuit 2019). The Northern Mariana Islands have a bicameral legislature; the 1975 Covenant was approved by 78.8% on 95% turnout; its delegate was first elected in 2008. The U.S. Virgin Islands have a unicameral legislature and citizenship since 1927; a 1981 proposed constitution was rejected by voters. All four have a nonvoting delegate and no presidential electors. Admission authority: Article IV s3; D.C. electors: the 23rd Amendment.
